1:
Whether the first proverb contrasts a poor man with a rich one is less settled than it looks. Keil and Delitzsch observe that a parallel proverb states the contrast far more clearly, but refuse to correct this one into conformity with it, as one scholar would. They report the arguments that the man in the second line must be understood as rich, and that the ideas of a rich man and a despiser of God were early connected; they also report a reading taking the word for fool to mean one who makes riches his confidence, and reject it, the word denoting the intellectually slothful, in whom the flesh outweighs the mind. Wealth, on their account, attaches not to that word but to the phrase about perverse lips. Charles Ellicott takes the same phrase to mean one who distorts the truth, and thinks a rich man likely meant on the strength of the parallel passage. Matthew Henry ignores the question and expands the comparison: the poor man has a better character, is in a better condition, is better beloved, and lives to better purpose than many who look great and make a figure. John Gill puts it as a paradox, that a man may be poor in worldly things and rich towards God.

The next saying is disputed in rendering. Adam Clarke asks whether it would not be plainer, as it is more literal, to say that to be without knowledge is not good for the soul, and reports two ancient versions giving that it is not good for a man not to know his own soul, and an old English rendering that where there is no discretion the soul is unwell. Gill reports the same versions and adds a Jewish reading making the missing knowledge that of the law. Henry takes the received sense and presses it inward—know we not our own hearts?—and closes with a maxim: it is as good not to know as not to consider. On the hasty feet Ellicott and Clarke agree that the man misses the mark he aims at, Clarke adding that a child does nothing cautiously because uninstructed, and a man without the knowledge of God is incautious and headstrong in the same way.

The two remaining sayings are read as one lesson about blame. Keil and Delitzsch note that the verb’s root idea is the reversal of a natural order and that the way here is the course of a life; the man is himself the fabricator of his own ruin, yet the ill-humour of his heart turns against God, so that he blames God rather than his own madness, which had turned grace into licence and cast away the instruction lying in providences. Henry says the same—it is their own iniquity that corrects them—and adds that in fretting we become enemies to our own peace and self-tormentors. John Wesley puts it in a line, that the man ascribes his unhappiness not to his sin but to providence, and Clarke exclaims at the inconsistency. On wealth and friends Keil and Delitzsch make a grammatical point with a moral edge: the accentuation shows the poor man is not the one separated but that his friend separates himself, and were the poor man made the subject the initiative of the desertion would not be expressed at all. Ellicott renders it so too, and observes that the merciful provisions of the law were laid on the people precisely to counteract these selfish instincts. Henry describes the mechanism—wealth enables a man to send presents and make entertainments, so that men flatter him while really loving what he has, or rather themselves—and catches the excuse that follows the reversal: since conscience tells men they ought to relieve such a case, they are glad to say they did not see it. Gill quotes a poet: while a man is fortunate he will count many friends.
5:
On the false witness Matthew Henry traces the road that leads there. No one could arrive at perjury, he says, without first allowing himself untruths in jest and banter, or under pretence of doing good; men teach their tongues to speak lies, and those who can swallow a false word debauch their consciences until a false oath will not choke them. What emboldens the offender is the hope of impunity, since this is a sin that commonly escapes punishment from men however strict the law may be—which is why the threat is doubled. John Gill completes the thought, that a man undetected here will not be undetected hereafter. Keil and Delitzsch notice the placing of the verse rather than its sense, observing that it and its near repetition further on open two groups of proverbs, and that the old Greek version, which elsewhere renders the phrase as kindling lies, varies its wording in both places to avoid repeating itself.

The courting of the generous man is described with unusual physical exactness. Keil and Delitzsch render the first line that many stroke the cheeks of the noble, deriving the verb from a root meaning to rub or stroke, whose cognates run out on one side to being weak and on the other to being sweet; and define the man so courted not merely as a prince but as one easily moved to noble actions, particularly to open-handedness, or naturally impelled that way. Henry draws the comparison out: liberality goes further than majesty itself in gaining respect, since many court a prince but every man is a friend to one who gives. He then divides the givers. Prodigals, foolishly free with what they have, gather hangers-on who cry them up while it lasts and leave when it is gone, whereas those who are prudently generous build an interest that may stand them in good stead and gain an authority by which they can do good. He turns the whole to account with a question—how earnest we should be for a favour so far beyond any earthly prince’s—and John Wesley adds the necessary qualification in three words, that such a friend is a friend in profession. Gill notes that the suitors themselves may be great men, courtiers seeking places.

The verse about the poor man’s brothers is defective, and the voices handle the defect differently. Charles Ellicott says plainly that the first half of a verse appears to have dropped out here, and offers a sense for what remains: the poor man hunts after words, seeking promises of help from his friends which end in nothing but talk. Keil and Delitzsch confine themselves to the first two lines, identifying the brothers as brothers by blood rather than the friend who has become a brother, and defending the accentuation against two scholars who would read a word differently. Adam Clarke corrects the strength of the verb: these men neither hate him positively nor love him, they simply disregard him and will have nothing to do with him, the word meaning not only to hate but to show a lesser degree of love to one than to another—as one patriarch is said to have hated the wife he loved less. Henry finds a second reading of the last clause that reverses the pursuit: it may be they who pursue him with words, excusing themselves from giving him anything by telling him he is idle and impertinent and has brought his poverty on himself. He closes by advising the poor to make God their friend and pursue him with prayers, and elsewhere observes that the one who was left by all his disciples had the Father with him still. Wesley reads the pursuit the usual way, as earnestly imploring their pity, and Gill says the brothers reckon him a reproach and do not choose to own him.
8:
The wisdom a man gets is located precisely. Charles Ellicott points out that the word is literally heart, and that a wisdom beginning in the fear of God and ending in loving him is no matter of intellect only but of the will and affections. John Gill reads it the same way and fills it out—a new heart, a heart of flesh in place of stone, sought after, prayed for and at last possessed. Matthew Henry works from the second clause: no man ever hated his own flesh, yet many are wanting in love to their souls, and only those love themselves rightly who get true wisdom and keep it. Keil and Delitzsch attend to the tense, taking the second line as a future periphrasis—it comes to this, that he acquires good—and observe that the division of conduct into care for the soul and its opposite runs through the book. When the warning against false witness returns, Henry notes it has gained a word: before, the liar was told he would not escape; now, that he will perish, the lies forged against others proving his own ruin. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the new verb as losing oneself in the place of the separated, and note the Greek used a plain negative first and a stronger word here.

On the fool in luxury they agree, then compete in illustration. Keil and Delitzsch quote a judgment that a fool cannot bear luxury but is made more foolish by it, and that a humble slave who attains prominence by good fortune turns at once from something good into something bad; the Greek, they add, read a different preposition and rendered the second line as ruling with insolence, where every other translator had the received text. Adam Clarke takes the first line of splendid living, rank and equipage, which sit ill on a fool though a lord by birth, and delivers two verdicts: he pities the king who puts himself into the hands of his own ministers, and thinks it worse when a man of mean extraction is raised to power, being generally cruel and tyrannical. Ellicott supposes an emancipated slave raised by court favour and trampling insolently on those once above him. Henry has the sharpest phrase—none are so insolent as a beggar on horseback—and the most careful distinction, that delight is seemly enough in a man of business to refresh him when fatigued, but not in a fool who lives idly and abuses his recreations. John Wesley gives the reason: prosperity corrupts even wise men and makes fools mad, and gives such a man more chance to discover his folly. Gill turns it to spiritual delight, which comes ill from those who talk of communion with God while living in sin.

The proverb on deferred anger is textually contested and morally applied. Keil and Delitzsch report that several old versions vocalised the phrase differently, giving long-suffering, and note that Jewish scholars have called that impossible; the sense is rather that a man’s discretion extends his anger, so that it is long in breaking out. Henry divides the deferral in two: put off admitting the anger until the provocation has been weighed, and put off acting on it until there is no danger of indecencies—he quotes a philosopher who told his servant he would beat him but that he was angry. Henry notices too how the second clause runs against instinct, since quickness to apprehend an affront is commonly counted ingenuity, whereas here the glory lies in appearing not to have seen it. Clarke turns the same clause on duelling, mimicking the man of honour who must have his adversary’s blood whatever God may say, and concluding that whoever sends a challenge should hang, since he intends murder. Ellicott says only that in forbearing a man imitates a Greater, and Gill that he is most like the God who defers his own anger.
12:
The king’s two moods are described, then applied in opposite directions. Keil and Delitzsch take the first word not as anger against a particular person but as general ill-humour, whose growling they compare to a lion setting itself to fall on its prey; against it stands the favour that makes everything live, like dew on the herbs of the field. The proverb, they say, states a fact, but so that the king may see himself in it. Matthew Henry turns the mirror both ways. It should make kings considerate in their frowns and smiles, since it concerns them never to frighten a good man from doing well nor countenance a wicked man in doing ill; and it should make subjects dutiful, restrained by the danger of having the government against them. Adam Clarke is blunter: the king above law, who rules without law and whose will is his own law, is exactly the lion, and this he thinks strongly descriptive of the sovereigns of the East. John Gill reports a Jewish reading taking the king here to be God himself.

The leaking roof is the figure everyone dwells on. Keil and Delitzsch explain the word as properly striking, stroke after stroke without interval, citing an old interpreter who glossed it as that which drops, and drops, and always drops; they also quote a proverb naming three things that make a house intolerable—rain trickling in, the contention of a wife, and bugs. Clarke draws the same picture: the man is a tenant whose cottage has a bad roof, so he can neither sit, work nor sleep out of reach of the drip, and ends by asking God’s help for anyone so placed, in house or in wife. Charles Ellicott notes the flat roof of an eastern house on a wet day. Henry generalises the pair of griefs into a proof of the world’s vanity, that we are liable to the greatest sorrow where we promise ourselves the greatest comfort, and notes that those used to chiding never want something to chide at.

That a good wife is not to be had by contrivance is the next point, and Henry presses it hardest. A woman always finding fault may take it for wisdom, but it is really her folly; and a man who has the opposite is not to credit his own choice, since the wisest have been deceived both in and by a woman. No man, he adds, has a good wife by descent or entail, and worldly parents who look no further than matching their children to house and riches should give God the glory if a prudent wife comes too. Keil and Delitzsch make the contrast structurally: house and riches, which do not of themselves make men happy, come by inheritance, while the wife comes by gift; no word could better characterise her, they say, quoting a saying that the quality it names wears the crown of all virtues. Clarke defines her dryly, as one of good understanding who avoids complaining though she may often have cause. On the sluggard, Clarke and Ellicott both notice that the sleep bears the word used of the first man’s, Ellicott preferring that it falls upon him rather than that he is cast into it. Keil and Delitzsch refuse a correction making the line mean slothfulness gives tasteless herbs to eat, and defend the Hebrew literature against a scholar who thought the Greek rendering of the word for sloth was needed to expose coarse verses, replying that it never sank so low and the Greek word meant no more than a weakling. Henry gives the sluggard his character—dozing away his time, burying his talents, an unprofitable burden of the earth who might as well be asleep for any service he does awake—and applies the hunger to the soul that takes no pains for salvation. Gill and Wesley say as much more briefly.
16:
Whose ways are despised in the sixteenth verse is not agreed. Charles Ellicott takes them for the man’s own, which he will not examine as to whether they please God, while John Wesley glosses the phrase as the commands of God, making both lines say the same thing. Keil and Delitzsch keep the received text against a conjecture giving he that scattereth his ways, of a man drawn now one way and now another by objects of sensuality; the emendation, they say, is foreign to this book and superfluous. Despising one’s way, on their account, is treating it as worth no consideration, no question of conscience which road to enter. Ellicott divides the death that follows into three: physical, spiritual, and one completed hereafter. Matthew Henry puts the promise the other way round, that if we keep God’s word his word will keep us from everything really hurtful, and cautions against abusing free grace as though it did away with the necessity of obedience. John Gill allows the commandment cannot be perfectly kept, and asks only that it be kept as far as a man is able.

The saying about lending to God draws the boldest language here. Adam Clarke exclaims at it: God makes himself debtor for everything given to the poor, and who would not advance much on such credit, since he has never once forfeited his word? Henry presses the figure further, noting that the verb means lending upon interest, and that the giver should take as much comfort in it as a moneylender who had placed a sum in good hands. Henry also catches a second sense in the last clause. The margin reads not what a man has given but what he has done, so that it is charity to do for the poor as well as give to them—which means the poor themselves, having limbs and senses, may be charitable to one another. Keil and Delitzsch trace the legal conception underneath, the contract by which a loan creates an obligation, and note that the construction makes God the party bound. Gill guards the motive, that the gift must come from true charity and not from a selfish principle, and Ellicott points to the one who became poor himself and counts what is done to a poor brother as done to him.

The command about chastening a son is where the chapter divides most sharply. Matthew Henry, Adam Clarke and John Wesley all keep the received sense of the second line, that a parent is not to be disarmed by the child’s crying. Henry warns against both delay and softness—correct the corrupt disposition before it takes root, since weeds are easiest plucked as they spring, and do not let a dissembled repentance buy off the correction, for better the child cry under a parent’s rod than under the sword of the magistrate. Clarke concedes it is a hard precept, nothing affecting a parent so much as a child’s tears, but sets against them the parent’s own tears afterwards, when the child is grown and his evil habits are sealed for life. Keil and Delitzsch read the clause quite differently. The soul is the object, not the subject, and to lift up the soul towards a thing is to set desire on it—so the line means, do not go so far as to kill him; correction is to be rigorous, but with wisdom and love setting its measure. Ellicott gives that rendering too, as a warning against zeal for the child’s good going too far or despairing of his amendment, and then adds a third possibility without deciding between them, that the words may equally mean, do not let him perish for want of chastisement. Gill fixes the time rather than the manner, that the hope lasts while the child is under parental government and before habits in sin have grown strong.
19:
The first word of the nineteenth verse defeats them. Keil and Delitzsch report that the written text yields no appropriate meaning, that three ancient versions read a different phrase, and that the margin gives great. They then dispose of two conjectures: a derivation from an Arabic word meaning stony, in a version they call after the heavy style of its author, and one from another meaning large, needing a change of letter they call physiologically undemonstrable and unsupported by any example worth mentioning. They allow the Hebrew may have had an adjective meaning gravel-like, and add drily that tow rather than gravel would suit the word for wrath. Matthew Henry offers two quite different readings. On the first, angry men never want woe, since if friends deliver them from one trouble they fall into another; on the second, which he thinks equally good, the wrathful man is the child of the previous verse crying against the rod, and delivering him for that outcry only means punishing him harder next time. Adam Clarke takes it of a surety called on again and again for the same friendly office, Charles Ellicott says we cannot shield wrong-headed people from the consequences of their own want of self-control, and John Wesley glosses deliver as forbearing to punish.

On hearing counsel Keil and Delitzsch correct a rendering: the phrase means not that a man may at last become wise, but henceforth—he must break with the undisciplined beginning of his life and be wise for the time remaining. Matthew Henry plays on the word—wise in the latter end and wise for it—and adds that those who would be stored in winter must gather in summer. Ellicott reads it as growth from a small beginning. The proverb on human devices they treat as its answer. Keil and Delitzsch find two things in the verb, that God’s counsel is accomplished and that it continues, and describe it as the one reality standing above the checkered manifoldness of human aims, so that a man’s thoughts gain unity and endurance only as he subordinates them to it. Henry sorts the devices into three kinds—against God’s counsels, without them, and unlike them—and notes the traffic runs one way: his counsel breaks men’s measures, but their devices cannot alter it or put him upon new ones, which checks politic men who suppose they can outwit all mankind. John Gill catalogues the devices, including religious ones, of men contriving new modes of worship and other methods of salvation.

The last verse of the group nobody settles. Keil and Delitzsch lay out four ways of taking the first line—what makes a man worthy of being desired, what adorns him, what men chiefly seek after, and, on an Aramaic sense of the second word, that a man’s pleasure is his disgrace—then examine the reading that what brings a man true joy is to act amiably. They ask whether that is true stated so generally, and object that if it were the thought a plainer word would have carried it; there they leave it. Ellicott offers two senses without choosing, that what makes a man beloved is his kindness, or that a man’s kindness consists in his good-will even where he cannot act on it. Henry states the second more warmly: better a heart to do good without the ability than ability without the heart, God and man alike accepting the good-will according to what a man has. On the comparison he is sharper—the character of low men, that they are vanity and nothing is expected of them, is better than that of high men, that they are a lie and deceive the expectations they raised. Wesley identifies the liar as the rich man who feeds the poor with promises he does not perform, and Gill reports a Jewish reading taking the first word in the sense of reproach, of the evil imaginations of the heart.
23:
The promise attached to the fear of God is read closely, then qualified. Keil and Delitzsch render the second line that one spends the night satisfied and unvisited by evil, the idiom meaning to pass the long night hungry: the man goes not to bed unfed nor fears waking in terror out of a soft slumber. Matthew Henry quotes the same in a Latin tag, that such a man shall not go supperless to bed, and divides the blessing into safety, satisfaction and happiness—the God-fearing may be visited with sickness, but with no evil in it, nothing to separate them from the love of God. Charles Ellicott marks a difference between the covenants here: a higher blessing is promised later, not immunity from trouble, which may be needed for advance in holiness, but protection within it. John Wesley and John Gill keep the promise simple: the man is contented with God’s favour, and the fear of God begins a spiritual life and is connected with the eternal one.

Where the sluggard puts his hand is disputed. Keil and Delitzsch note that if the word means bosom the saying is hyperbole, which is why the old Greek version rendered it lap, two later Greek translators the armpit, and Jewish interpreters the slit of a shirt; they prefer the figure of a dish, which elsewhere appears as a vessel wiped and turned upside down. Ellicott follows them: the dish set in the middle of an eastern table, into which guests dipped their hands for food. John Gill reports the same ambiguity, the word being sometimes used for a pot or platter, and canvasses hands under a vessel over the fire, hands over one set at a distance, and a hand put into a plate of food. Henry keeps the bosom and paints it: the man pretends he is lame, warms his hands and must then keep them warm, hugs himself in his ease and thinks there no such fine life as sitting still. Adam Clarke calls it strange that a man would rather starve than take the trouble of eating, and Henry adds that if those who will not labour must not eat, this one starves rather than stir, so his sin is his own punishment.

On smiting the scorner they agree the blow is not aimed at him. Keil and Delitzsch correct a rendering that would make the simple become prudent as a consequence, arguing the two verbs are joined to express simultaneity, and admit that with such a man, on whom denunciation bears no fruit and may work the contrary effect, nothing remains but to vindicate the injured truth by punishment—which may bring him wholesome terrors though he is not made better. Ellicott is franker: punishment will do the scorner no good, but may make the simple, whose character is not yet formed either way, reflect and amend; and God punishes sinners at first for their own sake, afterwards, when obdurate, as a warning to others. Henry puts it in a figure: if it cure not the infected it may prevent the spreading of the infection. On the second line all agree no blow is needed, Henry observing that a word to the wise is enough and Wesley that a verbal reproof does more for such a man than the severest punishment for a scorner. Gill draws the encouragement: though reproof is lost on one it succeeds in another. Of the son who wastes his father Clarke reports a textual difference: the common Latin reading has him expelling his mother, while his old English Bible followed a copy that had him shunning her and leaving her to penury—and he calls it a prostitution of the word to name such a creature a man. Henry describes both, the estate wasted and the mother made so weary of the house that she is glad to retire, then turned out at last.
27:
The twenty-seventh verse is read two opposite ways. Keil and Delitzsch take it as bitter irony: cease hearing instruction, if you will make no other use of it than to depart from the words of knowledge. On that reading it is no advice but a dissuasive from hypocrisy, a warning against the self-deception of the hearer who is no doer, and against heightening one’s condemnation by knowing the master’s will and not doing it. Charles Ellicott gives the same sense in a sentence: make up your mind now what you intend hereafter, since it is better not to know the truth than to learn it only to desert it. Matthew Henry takes it straight, as a caution to the well brought up against those who under pretence of instructing them draw them from good principles. He describes the trade exactly: the factors for vice undertake to teach a young man free thoughts and a fashionable conversation, how to palliate the sins he has a mind to and stop the mouth of his conscience, how to be quit of his education; and the wisdom of youth is to turn a deaf ear, as the adder to the charmer. John Gill reads it the same way and supplies a long polemical list of the teachers he has in view. Keil and Delitzsch note which construction the verb usually takes and what wording would have removed the ambiguity.

On the worthless witness the scholars work the second line. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the law knows no oath of witnesses, but that its adjuring them to speak truth puts a false statement almost in the rank of perjury, so that what the worthless witness scorns is his duty to state the matter without deceitful reservation. They then refuse an emendation reading justice for mischief, giving, the mouth of the wicked murders that which is right; its argument rests on the intensive form of the verb meaning annihilate, and they reply that the two forms interchange in the plain sense of swallowing, with no idea of destruction attached. Henry puts the scorn dramatically: tell such a man that law and equity, the scriptures and an oath are sacred things not to be jested with, and that a reckoning day is coming, and he laughs at it all. On the second line Henry has him drinking iniquity like water, Ellicott swallowing it as a dainty morsel, and John Wesley uttering it with greediness and delight. John Gill allows an alternative: instead of scoffing openly the man covers what is right and eludes judgment by specious arguments.

The last verse divides over whose judgments are meant. Keil and Delitzsch are emphatic that the word never means punishment inflicted by a court but always the judgments of God, even where inflicted through human agency; and they correct a remark that the judgment may consist in the stripes of an earlier verse. The stroke there, they say, is the blow given to one who despises what is holy, which may be salutary, and belongs to neither category here—the first being providential chastisements with which God in history visits the despiser of religion, the second the strokes laid on a fool’s back by one instructing him. Henry takes the civil sense and keeps the other besides: the magistrate has judgments prepared for scorners, since otherwise he would bear the sword in vain, but if he connives at sin, God’s judgments do not slumber. Adam Clarke reads it wholly of just laws, and advises avoiding such men’s company and their end. Gill states both plainly: judgments come by the magistrate or by the Lord, and indeed by both, so a man who misses one will meet the other. Wesley answers the delay: though deferred, they are treasured up. Henry closes on the certainty rather than the agent: the unbelief of man will not make the threatenings of no effect.
